lesson.title: Why Water Dissolves Almost Everything Life Needs
lesson.summary: Water is called the universal solvent because its polar structure lets it surround and separate charged or polar particles, dissolving the salts, sugars, and gases that life depends on for transport.
lesson.body:
A solvent is any substance capable of dissolving other substances, called solutes, into a uniform mixture called a solution. Water dissolves more different kinds of substances than any other common liquid, which is why chemists nickname it the universal solvent. That reputation is a direct consequence of the polarity already discussed: because a water molecule carries a partial negative charge on its oxygen and partial positive charges on its hydrogens, it can position itself around charged or polar particles and pull them apart from each other.

Table salt, sodium chloride, demonstrates the mechanism clearly. In dry crystal form, positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions are locked together in a rigid lattice held by strong ionic bonds. Drop that crystal into water and the polar water molecules attack the lattice from every side: the oxygen ends of water molecules cluster around each sodium ion, and the hydrogen ends cluster around each chloride ion. Enough of these attractions accumulate to overcome the ionic bonds holding the crystal together, and individual ions peel away, each one surrounded by a shell of oriented water molecules called a hydration shell. The salt has dissolved, not by being destroyed, but by being pulled apart and stabilized ion by ion.

Water performs the same trick with polar molecules that carry no full charge, such as sugars, because their oxygen and hydrogen groups also carry partial charges that water molecules can hydrogen bond with directly. Its reach has limits, though. Nonpolar substances like vegetable oil have no charge separation for water to grab onto, so water molecules would rather hydrogen bond with each other than surround an oil molecule, and the two liquids separate instead of mixing. This distinction, what water will and will not dissolve, sets up the difference between hydrophilic and hydrophobic substances covered next.

This solvent property is how transport works inside every organism. Blood plasma is mostly water, and it carries dissolved glucose, amino acids, hormones, and ions like sodium, potassium, and calcium to every tissue in the body, each one hydrated and mobile rather than locked in a crystal or clump. Oxygen and carbon dioxide, though less soluble in water than ions or sugars, still dissolve enough to be carried in blood and to diffuse across the thin, moist surfaces of lungs and gills.

The same chemistry operates in soil. Mineral nutrients such as nitrate, potassium, and magnesium are typically bound in soil particles or salts, but rainwater dissolves them into the soil solution, and plant roots draw up that dissolved nutrient-rich water rather than absorbing solid minerals directly. Without water's ability to pull ions and polar molecules apart and hold them in solution, nutrients could not move from soil to root, from gut to bloodstream, or from bloodstream to cell. Water's solvent power is, in a very real sense, the delivery system that makes multicellular life logistically possible.
